extracted.intended_audience: instructors and advanced undergraduate/graduate students in discrete mathematics, graph theory, and computational chemistry (benzenoids); also readers implementing LZ'77 and trie/suffix structures
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques, definitions, and formulae for counting perfect matchings in hexagonal systems (benzenoids) including special classes (linear chains, rectangular, parallelogram, fibonaccene, tubulenes) and a determinant-based method; plus an instructional discussion of tries/suffix trees and the LZ'77 compression scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a hexagonal system
rubrics_metrics.description: A hexagonal system is a 2-connected planar graph such that each interior face can be drawn as a regular hexagon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This condition forces all vertex degrees in a hexagonal system to be 3 or 2 (and only 2 on the exterior boundary). Moreover, every pair of adjacent hexagons have exactly one edge in common. All hexagonal systems in the article are drawn with two vertical edges.

rubrics_metrics.name: 2-connectedness and structural implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Hexagonal systems are required to be 2-connected (connected and at least two vertices must be removed to disconnect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: vertex degrees constrained (3 or 2); exterior vertices degree 2; adjacency between hexagons as single shared edge. Useful when arguing existence of perfect matchings and for inductive proofs on hexagon counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bipartiteness of hexagonal systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Every hexagonal system is bipartite (can partition vertices into black and white sets B and W).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be proved by induction on number of hexagons (exercise). Bipartiteness is necessary to define the biadjacency matrix and to apply the determinant formula; also implies that a perfect matching requires equal-sized parts B and W.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity requirement for perfect matchings
rubrics_metrics.description: A graph must have an even number of vertices in order to contain a perfect matching; if G has 2n vertices then any perfect matching M has exactly n edges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple necessary condition frequently used to rule out existence of perfect matchings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear chain perfect-matching count
rubrics_metrics.description: A linear chain of length h (h hexagons with adjacent pairs sharing a vertical edge and no nonvertical edges) has exactly h+1 perfect matchings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a one-to-one correspondence between perfect matchings in a linear chain and its vertical edges; linear chains serve as building blocks for larger hexagonal systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rectangular hexagonal system count (Theorem 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the rectangular hexagonal system R[h,v], the number of perfect matchings is (h+1)^v.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: none of the vertical edges from certain rows can be used in a perfect matching (coloring argument on top linear chain), so perfect matchings factor as product of perfect matchings of constituent linear chains; since each Li has h+1 matchings, take product over v chains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallelogram hexagonal system count (Theorem 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the parallelogram hexagonal system P[h,v], the number of perfect matchings is C(h+v, v) (binomial coefficient).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by induction on v using decomposition of matchings depending on presence/absence of particular boundary edges; uses Pascal's Identity. Theorem gives combinatorial equivalences (e.g., with lattice paths and non-decreasing sequences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fibonaccene chain recurrence (Theorem 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a fibonaccene chain H with h hexagons, the sequence a_h = (number of perfect matchings) satisfies a_h = a_{h-1} + a_{h-2} with initial values a1 = 2, a2 = 3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hence counts follow Fibonacci-like sequence; proofs and exercises derive small-term values and variants (e.g., adding a hexagon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tubulene/tubulene count (Theorem 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a tubulene hexagonal system T[h,k] (rectangular hexagonal system embedded on a cylinder with k rows), the number of perfect matchings is 2^{k+1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Property: (cid:30).T[h;k] is independent of horizontal length h and depends only on k; gluing boundary vertical edges reduces the count compared to the unglued rectangular case. Proof left as exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kekulé index (stability/energy measure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given hexagonal system H with number of hexagons f(H), the Kekulé index is defined as log2(#perfect_matchings(H)) / f(H).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This index is interpreted as an 'average resonance energy per hexagon' and is used to compare chemical stability: higher Kekulé index (higher energy) implies less stability. Examples compare R[5,4] and T[5,7].

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinant formula for counting perfect matchings (Theorem 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a hexagonal system H (bipartite with equal sized B and W), the number of perfect matchings equals |det A(H)| where A(H) is the biadjacency matrix.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kasteleyn's result: nonzero terms in expansion of det correspond to perfect matchings and all such terms have the same sign so absolute value of determinant counts matchings. Implementation notes: labeling vertices and constructing A(H) (an n x n matrix) is the main work; computing determinant yields count (example: a 32x32 determinant gave 1,764).

rubrics_metrics.name: Biadjacency matrix construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct A(H) as the n x n biadjacency matrix with rows indexed by black vertices b1..bn and columns by white vertices w1..wn where a_{ij} = 1 if bi is adjacent to wj and 0 otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires B and W to have the same number of vertices (necessary for perfect matching existence). When building A(H) be careful with consistent labeling; determinant calculation uses standard permutation expansion interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computational complexity context
rubrics_metrics.description: Counting perfect matchings (the function #PM(G)) is computationally difficult in general: computing #PM(G) is NP-hard (remains true even for bipartite graphs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation for focusing on special planar classes (hexagonal systems) where efficient/countable formulas exist (e.g., determinants, closed forms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical prerequisites and recommended classroom use
rubrics_metrics.description: Intended as enrichment for an advanced discrete mathematics course; students should be familiar with counting techniques, graphs and determinants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructor guidance: give the paper to students to read, present a summary near course end, spend roughly one class meeting on it; exercises and selected solutions reinforce ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trie insertion and representation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: When embedding binary strings into a trie: every node has at most two children; insert each string at the minimal depth necessary so it is distinguished from others; use left branch for '0' and right branch for '1'; leaves have no children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields an unambiguous efficient embedding; useful background before discussing suffix trees and LZ'77. Examples illustrate how common prefixes create shared internal nodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suffix tree construction from suffixes of a word
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a binary word X, form suffixes S1 = X, S2 = X with first char removed, etc.; construct the trie (suffix tree) using the same insertion rules so common prefixes group suffixes together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suffix trees make visible the relationships among suffixes and motivate the LZ'77 compression step of finding long common prefixes with earlier suffixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: LZ'77 compression triple (core compression step)
rubrics_metrics.description: To compress the next uncompressed suffix S_{n+1}, find earlier suffix S_{i+1} with maximal common prefix of length L, then store three items: pointer to the start of S_{i+1} (i.e., Xi+1), the length L of the common prefix, and the next character X_{n+L+1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encoding the next character avoids the algorithm 'getting stuck' and is crucial to LZ'77; for Markov-generated sources this scheme is provably efficient. Examples show how this compresses blocks by referencing earlier occurrences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of suffix-tree neighborhood for candidate matches
rubrics_metrics.description: The parent (or ancestor) node of an uncompressed suffix in the suffix tree has descendants which are appropriate candidates Si for performing compression (i.e., those sharing the observed prefix).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawing suffix trees helps identify which earlier strings are valid pointers for LZ'77; examples show sibling/ancestor relationships (e.g., S7 and S13 being siblings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity/matching multiplicity and error-correction addendum
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple valid i produce the same maximal prefix (i.e., multiplicity > 1), this multiplicity matching parameter allows some error-correction during compression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This leads to research directions (author's Ph.D. thesis): the number of available Si's determines how much error correction can be performed; references given for deeper study.
